nameStory: The Two-colored Tube-web Spider gets its name from its striking two-toned appearance - a yellowish-brown front half and purplish-brown rear end. The genus name Ariadna comes from Greek mythology, referring to Ariadne who helped Theseus navigate the labyrinth, much like how these spiders create their own tunnel-like homes.
description: The Two-colored Tube-web Spider is a medium-sized spider that lives in silk-lined tunnels and burrows. Its most distinctive feature is its two-toned coloring: the front portion (cephalothorax) and legs are yellowish-brown, while the abdomen is a rich purplish-brown. These spiders are homebodies that rarely venture far from their tube-like retreats, preferring to wait for prey to come to them.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Distinctive two-tone coloring with yellowish-brown front section and legs contrasting sharply with a purplish-brown, often velvety-looking abdomen

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates silk-lined tubes in crevices, holes, or underground burrows rather than typical webs - look for funnel-like openings with silk around the entrance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely reclusive, staying deep in their tubes during the day and rarely seen in the open - they respond very slowly to disturbances

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, robust build with a relatively wide cephalothorax and rounded abdomen that feels firm to the touch if handled

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in protected spaces like rock crevices, old wood with holes, or artificial structures with small cavities they can line with silk

habitat: Two-colored Tube-web Spiders seek out protected spaces with existing holes or crevices they can convert into silk-lined retreats. Look for them in old wooden structures, rock walls, stone foundations, and even artificial habitats like drilled wood blocks. They prefer stable environments where they can establish permanent residences.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering sites and begin establishing new territories. This is when you're most likely to find them moving between locations.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're actively hunting from their established tubes. Mating occurs during warm summer months.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare overwintering sites and may be found creating more permanent tube retreats. Young spiders disperse to find their own territories.
seasonality.winter: Remain hidden deep in their silk-lined retreats, becoming completely inactive and nearly impossible to detect.

funFact: These spiders are so committed to their tube lifestyle that when researchers tested their response to food odors, they reacted in 63 seconds when outside their tubes but completely ignored the same smells when safely inside - they're literally nose-blind when at home!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small wolf spiders due to their brownish coloring, but tube-web spiders have that distinctive purplish abdomen and live in silk-lined retreats rather than hunting in the open. Remember: if it's in a tube, it's likely your spider!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "tube-web" spiders, they don't build traditional webs at all - they're tunnel architects instead. The family name Segestriidae refers to their unique lifestyle of living in silk-lined retreats, which is quite different from most other spider families.
compareHints: This is the only Ariadna species commonly found in New England, making identification easier once you recognize the tube-dwelling lifestyle. Compared to other tunnel spiders in the family, the Two-colored Tube-web Spider is distinguished by its specific yellowish-brown and purplish-brown color pattern and its willingness to use artificial structures as nesting sites.
